speechtext: No, I have covered that case by the first amendment, and I have covered the other case by the second amendment. If you ask fhat any other case be provided for, I will cover that by a few more words.

I think it will be admitted that the wise policy is to give recognition to Canadians who went to South Africa in Canadian forces. It does not seem to me that it is wise to extend this privilege beyond the men who went out in Canadian regiments. I think this right of recognition should not depend upon whether these men actually went into battle or served in any particular engagement, but that those who left the shores of Canada to go to South Africa to fight and were prepared to fight if necessary, should receive recognition. If you take the case of men who chose to go over to England and enlisted in English regiments you are dealing with men who did not go as Canadians, and I therefore think that this recognition should be confined to those who went and served as Canadians.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to correct him?

I was not referring to the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Stanfield), but the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron)-the case of a man living in the Northwest who went over and enlisted in an English regiment.
At the time this man cabled to England for permission to join the forces he did not know that we were going to send troops from Canada.

If you deal with cases of that kind, you will have all kinds of excuses which no department could follow up in order to arrive at a proper basis for determining who should be entitled to this grant. There may be cases of officers who served with distinction who being Canadians served in the

Imperial forces and wlio are deserving of recognition, and those can be dealt with separately. But if - we are dealing with non-commissioned officers and men, I think this country would only be disposed to give recognition to Canadians who went as members of Canadian forces.

Take three cases that I have in mind; one was that of Charlie Boss, of the Northwest Mounted Police, the scout, and the man who won the battle at Cut Knife Hill in 18S.1. Charlie Ross went to South Africa and did splendid service. But the particular cases that I have in mind are those of two young men in Toronto-Wasson and Jackson. These two men could not get into the first corps. They were away earning their living and not within reach of their regiments. They started back to the regimental headquarters, but when they arrived the corps were tfilled. They went to South Africa in a hay ship. I could give the name of another young fellow, Charley Graham, from my own town of Lindsay who also went out in a hay ship. They joined Roberts' forces, and by their conduct reflected credit on the name of Canada. Yet these men would be excluded under this resolution.
Where are you going to draw the line?
Any Canadian who served in any corps in South Africa. Take the case of Colonel Hamilton Merritt, of Toronto ; he served on General Brabant's staff.
You are included.
Certainly. I could not go to South Africa because of. the tyranny of an English general who was serving under the Canadian government.
I would like to ask the minister if a man availing himself of his privilege and locating on land would be entitled to a homestead and to a pre-emption also?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provisions of this Bill admit of a volunteer or his assignee getting the full benefit of the Act whether he has already a homestead or not.
Or whether he is going to get one?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes ; it is precisely the same thing.
You are going to allow a man to have a homestead in addition to this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And a pre-emption, too?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If he takes it in a preemption area.
You will give him a whole square mile of land? He will be glad to see another war break out.
I have given notice of an amendment to this motion. The minister has made some change in. it, but I have something to add when the time comes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think we had better allow clause 2 of the resolution to stand and proceed with the Bill. We can have an opportunity to redraft clause 2.
Section 2 allowed to stand.
On section 3-grants of land authorized.

would like to move an amendment to that section as follows :
That the word ' volunteer,' in the first line of clause 3, be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor: ' officer, non-commissioned officer Or man, or in the event of his death, between the date of his enlistment or appointment and December 31, 1910, to his legal -representative.'
What will be the necessary procedure for a widow to take in order to get this land grant ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: She would simply have to establish her identity and the rights of her husband before tbe Militia Department.

Before that section carries, I have given notice of an amendment to this clause, and I think it is necessary to put it in here. I propose that clause 3 be amended by inserting after the word ' volunteer ' the words ' legal representative,' by striking out the word ' adjoining ' as it appears in the second line, and by providing that it shall apply to odd and even numbered sections all over the country. The Land Bill we have just passed may possibly have a hearing on clause 3.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under this provision and under the Land Bill the volunteer may take his land anywhere on the odd or even-numbered sections or on adjoining odd or even sections, but it does not provide for him taking them up except they do adjoin.

The South African veterans are generally residents in portions of the country that are well settled, and if a man could get a quarter-section in his locality, even though it did not adjoin his own quarter-section, it would be far better to let him have it than to compel him to move 100 miles away.
I cannot see why the nurses who accompanied the physicians to South Africa should not get a land grant. Does this clause include the chaplains ?
If they were enlisted it would.
The minister should take into consideration the question of including the nurses.

I would move that section 3 be amended by striking out the word 1 adjoining.' I believe the word ' adjoining ' will work very great hardship in the cases I have referred to. I do not see what difference it makes to the country whether the South African veteran gets his quarter-section adjoining his own, or whether he gets it some other place in the neighbourhood.
The hon. gentleman is legislating for an exceptional case instead of for a general one.
It is so general that it will apply to more than half the volunteers who are residents of that country.

McCarthy. If the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was at all familiar with the conditions in the Northwest he would understand that it is very difficult to get quarter-sections adjoining each other. The Bill now practically amounts to nothing, so far as a number of young men residents of Alberta and Saskatchewan who went to South Africa are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the opinion of the House is that the Bill amounts to nothing there are many people in the country who would much prefer to see the Bill withdrawn.

McCarthy. I am certainly not of the opinion that the Bill should be withdrawn. On the contrary, I have _ advocated in this House for several sessions the granting of land to the South African volunteers of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I am not speaking of the men who enlisted from other provinces and who received grants from Ontario and British Columbia, but I do think some provision should be made to set aside a grant of land to the young men who went to South Africa from the western provinces. What I want to point out to the minister is that if a man takes up a quarter-section under this Act he has to comply with the regulations of the homestead law. and while that may be well enough for a farmer or a rancher who wants to get more land, still there are many young men in the cities, towns, and villages who cannot leave their business, and the only benefit of this Act to them is that that they will get scrip for $160, which if they can sell for $80 they will be lucky. I have protests from this class of veterans and at the proper stage I shall move amendments to the Bill. That is what I intended to convey when I said that'the grant to this class of young men in Alberta and Saskatchewan has been practically whittled down to nothing.

I do not see why a South African veteran should be allowed to locate on two separated quarter-sections any more than you should allow a homesteader who has the privilege -of taking out
a pre-emption to do so. There will be millions of acres of land available for the South African veterans, and I do not think there is any hardshio whatever if they have to locate on quarter-sections adjoining. Let me point out to my hon. friend (Mr. M. S. McCarthy) that if the veteran does not want to live on the land and earn the patent by performing homestead duties, it is not necessary for him to take $160 in scrip. He can take his warrant which he has the privilege of selling and his assignee has the privilege of locating on two quarter-sections and performing the homestead duties and having the patent issued in his own name.
I believe the warrant will be worth more to him than a separate patent for a quarter-section.
Suppose a volunteer does not want to take 320 acres and go and farm it, but prefers to take the 160 acres, what title would he have to the 160 acres? Would he get scrip for it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has the chance of taking 320 acres as a homestead, or the chance of assigning his right to another person who will fulfil the duties on the 320 acres; the effect of which is, as my hon. friend from East Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has said, to give him a free patent for 160 acres, or scrip to the amount of $160, which is receivable at its face value in payment for Dominion lands.
How would the assignment be equal to 160 acres?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In this way, that whoever he assigns to gets 320 acres for fulfilling the duties that are required of a homesteader on 160 acres.
Amendment of Mr. Herron negatived.
On section 4-conditions.

I do not think you should allow a substitute. I think there should be just two alternatives; either give the man a grant if he wants to go to the land himself, or give him the scrip if he does not want to go on the land. But do not allow a substitute to take up the land, because the result will be that these rights will be sold for a trifle, especially by many eastern men, to some person who has never been in South Africa, but who will reap all the benefits barring the few dollars he pays for the right. If the volunteer himself wants to go on the land and fulfil the conditions, let him have the 320 acres. If not, let him take the $160 of scrip which he can use as he likes.
Suppose a man entitled to the 320 acres could not conveniently go on the land himself, could he place somebody else there to do the work for him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not unless he assigns his rights to that other person.
Suppose lie had a brother who would do the work on it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter that he aud his brother would have to arrange between them; but he would have to assign his rights to his brother. It seems to me that the opportunity given in the section as it stands is all that can reasonably be asked.

I presume that the general purpose under this Bill is to reward Canadians who have served the empire in South Africa; but in addition to that you desire if possible to get these good Canadians to settle in the Northwest, for various reasons that will suggest themselves. A young- man who is sufficiently loyal to risk his life in South Africa is a pretty good kind of man to mix with certain elements that will go into that country. Therefore it is desirable to do everything in our power to get that youug man to go out thpre and settle; but the idea of a substitute does not appear to fulfil the purpose of the Bill, and I agree with the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) that if he will not go out and take up the land and become a settler, we would do well to drop the provision for a substitute and let him accept the scrip.

Could the minister not arrange to diminish the number of months the veteran is required to remain on land? A man who has served his country for three years in South Africa in such an nHnnns way should not. I think, be bound to remain so long on the land. I think It would be sufficient to require him to remain three months on the land to do his settlement duties. I am in favour of seeing that the settlement duties are effectually done. It will not do to allow the land to lie vacant, and if necessary he could make up for the diminished time the veteran would have to be on the land by doing an extra amount of settlement duties. A good many veterans might remain three months on the land, but could not conveniently stay the whole summer. It would make very little difference to the country so long as the settlement duties were thoroughly done. These veterans should certainly get some advantage in this respect. And the time limit should not be so strictly enforced against them, considering the 'time they have already served their King and country.

I am very glad that the hon. member for East Huron (Mr Chisholm) has brought up that point. I might draw the minister's attention to the American regulations at the close of the Cuban and Philippine war. The volunteers on their return were each handed their scrip, and the time they had served in the campaign was counted in their homestead duties.
I believe in being generous to the young men who went out to

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: South Africa to fight the battles of the empire, and I think the provisions of this Bill are very generous. Under it, as I understand, a South African veteran can take up 320 acres of land as a veteran; he can then take 160 acres more as an ordinary homesteader, which gives him 480 acres; then by paying $480 he can pre-empt another 160 acres, which gives him 640 acres, or a mile square, for the small sum of $480. I think we are dealing pretty generously with these South African veterans without letting up at all on the homestead conditions. It would be much better for you to give a cash bonus to the veteran than permit him to sell his rights to some person and thus let some one who never made any sacrifice whatever get all the benefit. The provisions of the Bill are quite broad and generous enough and you should strike out the substitute.

I presume that the object is to recognize the services of the volunteers who went to South Africa, and I do not think this recognition would be of much value to them if they could not hold their land by engaging others to do the settlement duties. There are many of the volunteers engaged in other business besides farming, and this grant would be of no advantage to them if they were not allowed to provide a substitute. I think this Bill Is not too liberal and that you might go a little further. No doubt many of these volunteers would appreciate very much having a farm of 160 acres, and if they could, without giving up their business, go out there and work a short time on the land or engage others to break it up for farming, they would hold it for all time to come and hand it down to their children as a memento of the services they had performed. I think they should be given the advantage of holding their land without having to give up their business connection in other parts of the country. Those Canadians who went to South Africa made their mark there; they won several battles, and to a certain extent taught the British soldiers how to fight and how to manage without exposing themselves unnecessarily, as British soldiers were accustomed to do. In fact, they introduced a new life into the army of that country. It is a pity this Bill does not deal witli them more liberally by enabling them to hold their land without breaking up their business.

I would like to hear an expression of opinion from the minister with regard to this question. We know what has been the fate of this scrip in the past. Scrip speculators went over the country and bought the scrip for a mere song and many made large fortunes out of it. In like manner fortunes will be made, though in a smaller degree, by men who have no title to any recognition. Take this land a mile square to-day, that is worth $3,000 or $4,000, and you are giving it for

the price value of the scrip. In a few years it will he worth $25,000 to $30,000.

I do not think the question of a man's right to homestead and preemption need be mixed up with this at all. You are giving a veteran, something for his work in South Africa. If he has had a homestead, he cannot get another. If he has not you cannot, when giving him something you say he is entitled to, cut him out of his right to a homestead. As regards the cutting down of the settlement duties, that would be most unsatisfactory. You are giving a half-section, half a mile wide by a mile long, to a South African veteran, and he has to do the necessary homestead duties and six months residence each year for three years. It would be most unsatisfactory to other settlers in the vicinity if he could earn his patent by doing less homestead duties-if, for instance, he could earn it by a three months' residence or less, or by doing the cultivation duties instead of residence. I agree with the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fowler) that they are being dealt with liberally. They are being given half a section instead of the quarter-section, which was what most of them expected, and I do not think we are asking too much if we ask that they should perform' the necessary homestead conditions. Then as regards doing away with the right to substitute ; a substitute may be just as good a settler, and that is one of the chief objects the government has in view, namely, that in giving this land to the South African veterans you ensure that the land will be occupied, cultivated and settled upon.

What the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fowler) said about the scrip holder in days gone by selling his scrip is absolutely true, because very few people could be induced in those days to go and settle in the Northwest, but it is entirely different to-day. I know hundreds of boys who are just waiting for this scrip to go up and settle in the country. Many no doubt will sell their scrip, but there are scores who will go there and settle.
My suggestion will not apply to them.
The young fellows in the towns who cannot afford to go out should not be discriminated against.

There should be a distinction between a man who is a resident and a man who has never been in that country. Partially the object of giving this land is to promote the settlement of the Northwest, and I think that a man who has not been there, either before, during or since the war, should be asked to go and reside there either on his land or at least in the country.

The best plan to adopt is to compel the volunteer to settle on the
land or take his scrip. Otherwise you will have' the land sold and held vacant by speculators for many years to come. In the case of scrip given after the Riel rebellion not one in a hundred of those who were entitled to it and received it settled on the land. The scrip was sold as low as $10 to $15. I tried to sell mine and all I was offered for it was $15. The hon. member for Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes) says he knows of hundreds of boys who will go out and settle on the land. Well, that is the best argument we can have for making them settle on it or take their scrip.

The Ontario government have dealt more generously with the veterans in that province, they have exempted the land granted to them from taxation, except for school purposes, for ten years, and if the grantees do not settle on the land the government buys it back, sometimes of course for a small amount, $50 or $100. I do not think that this government would be wise in following their example and exempting the lands in the west from settlement duties. Even in New Ontario that retarded settement to such an extent that the Ontario government would probably not do it again.
There was some reason for the Ontario government granting this exemption from duties as they valued the land at only $50.

I do not think we should make the restrictions so very onerous. The idea in my mind is that these volunteers should be induced to settle there but you must not place too many restrictions on their mode of settlement. I have heard it suggested, and I think it is a good idea, that the nurses and chaplains who attended to the spiritual wants of the volunteers should have land as well, but I do not see how you could force these to live for six months on the land. If you make the conditions very onerous you force the grantees to take scrip, and we know that in the past many people have made it a trade to go to the west and deal in scrip. In many cases the grantees would sell their lands for very small amounts. I would again urge consideration for the chaplains and nurses, those who went there in any capacity to serve their country in the hour of need. Their action gave Canada more standing in history than perhaps any other event in the last twenty years. It will redound to the credit of this parliament to deal very generously with those volunteers. If I had my will about it I would do away with the scrip altogether. I do not think it is a fair or a good way to do the business. Some system of permitting substitutes to take the land might be adopted. I have heard this evening of a man who is ready to sell his claim for $25 and I have no doubt that some men will be ready to buy scrip at that rate.

As reference has been made to the Ontario Act I may quote from it :
Any person who was resident in the province and who went from the province to South Africa, to act as chaplain or nurse or Red Cross commissioner or a newspaper correspondent during the said war or any period thereof

These classes are allowed land under the Ontario Act. I think this is an example that might worthily be followed in the passage of this Bill.

Reverting to clause 2, I know a young man, Mr. Muckle, who happened to be visiting in New Zealand when the war broke out. He volunteered in the New Zealand contingent, fought through the war and immediately returned to his birthplace in Manitoba and resides there.
There is a similar case in Port Arthur of a young man named Gil-lis who was in South Africa and volunteered there.

I wish to offer an amendment to clause 4 beginning at the sixth line.
I move :
That clause 4 be amended by adding thereto the words: But this section shall not apply, in so far as residence and cultivation are required, to persons incapacitated as mentioned in section 2 thereof.
The effect of this amendment is that persons incapacitated in the war may get their land without settlement duties. There are a few special cases known to every member in this House. There are a few'men in my own county and if they were explained to the committee I am sure the committee would have no hesitation in adopting this amendment. There are not more than ten or twelve such cases in Canada.
Can a person entitled to this land assign it to any other person who must perform the duties, or would the man purchasing scrip be considered a grantee ?

With regard to scrip, we must all admit that in by-gone years there was a great deal of improper handling of scrip. It was no doubt bought up at very low prices, sometimes for a mere song. People there made it a business to gather up large quantities of this scrip, and buy large tracts of land with it, notably, I understand, the Saskatchewan Land Valley Company, in the purchase of 250,000 acres used a large amount of scrip. I do not think it is right that any person outside the volunteers themselves should get any advantage out of that scrip. The minister should so arrange the law that no person would he allowed to apply that scrip in the purchase of land unless he is prepared to make an affidavit that he paid the full $160 for it. I do not believe in these speculators in scrip being allowed to gather ' Mr MARTIN (Queens, P.E.TJ
it up at a mere nominal price, and then come to the government and purchase land with it, dollar for dollar.

That cash scrip at the present time would have a market value of between 90 and 95 per cent, so any one that took scrip good for the payment of $100 for Dominion lands, would be able to sell it for about $150. There is a good demand for the scrip on the part of those who have payments to make to the Dominion government, so any one who took that scrip would he sure to get close to $150 in cash for it. Of course, you can make a regulation that the purchaser must pay the full $160, but if you do there will be no sale for the scrip, because if any one had $160 to pay to the government, unless he could make five, six or seven per cent on the scrip, he would not bother buying it but pay cash instead. But there is so little of that class of scrip to be had, that he would not he sure of getting over 90 per cent for its face value.

There is another class of people that have been overlooked in the enumeration of those who ought to be entitled to a land grant, I refer to the newspaper correspondents. Like the soldiers, they went out to that country and took their lives in their hands, and they did more to advertise the country probably than the volunteers did. In my opinion they should receive recognition in this Bill.
With reference to some of the contingents who went out to South Africa, and did not serve, and then returned, will they be entitled ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter for consideration under clause 2, which has been hung up in deference to the unanimous view of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
A difficulty about the amendment of my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron) has been brought to my attention, namely, that section 2 is not yet amended, and the amendment which is proposed to section 2 would not be relevant there. I would suggest that my hon. friend's amendment be in the following terms :
" But this section shall not apply in so far as residence and cultivation are required, to persons who, -by reason of physical or mental incapacity arising from service in South Africa as aforesaid, are unable to comply with the conditions -as -to -residence and cultivation prescribed in section i hereof.
The object the hon. gentleman desires to attain is this, that the conditions as to residence and cultivation should not be imposed upon persons who, by reason of physical injuries or mental condition arising from the war, are unable to perform the duties which otherwise they would be required to perform under the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the provisions of the Dominion Lands Act would be sufficient to meet the cases suggested. Beyond that point it would be dangerous to go. The provisions of the Land Act are framed to meet just such cases as my hon. friend has in mind. I think it would be safer to leave such cases to the operation of the Dominion Lands Act.
(Mr. R. L. BORDEN. The minister then is satisfied that the provisions of the Lands Act would amply cover the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say they would amply cover the case, but I think they would cover it so far as it would be safe to go in administration ; otherwise we might have to deal with what might amount to a scandal in the matter of medical certificates and other means of avoiding settlement duties.	[DOT]

I had in mind one or two very severe cases in which I thought the applicant should get his patent forthwith without putting in the necessary three years. I have a case in mind where the man has been in the hospital ever since the end of tlie war, and he has a large family of ten children. I only know of two cases, but they are very special ones. I had them in view, and thought that they should be entitled to get their patents without performing the homestead duties. Does the minister think such a case could be dealt with in section 2 ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think clause 4 as it stands should be carried. The cases my hon. friend suggests can be met to a measurable degree under the provisions of the Dominion Lands Act. I could not support his amendment.
Perhaps the minister would not mind explaining what the provisions of the Lands Act are with respect to that particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
One provision is that where a homesteader is physically incapacitated from fulfilling his duties, by order of the Governor in Council, he may be granted a patent without residence.
On section 5-substitutes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have an amendment to clause 5 that I propose shall be added as subclause 3 as follows :
No such instrument shall be accepted or recognized by the department which is not executed and dated after the date of the warrant of the Minister of Militia and Defence, provided for in section 7 of this Act.

I would like an explanation from the minister as to what the addition to this clause means. I believe there are cases in the country in which some men have made arrangements to dispose of their
land. I suppose this is what it has reference to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amendment I have moved is for the purpose that is set forth in its wording, that the assignment of the volunteer is of no value until this right has been accorded by tbe Department of Militia and Defence; that is to say that the trafficking in rights which is going on at the present time will be at the loss of the enterprising purchaser and not at the loss of the volunteer.

I think there should be a change made in section 5. It reads :
No person 'shall be accepted as a substitute unless be is a British subject.
It is perfectly right that a man must be a British subject before a patent issues to him, but I do not see any more reason why a settler who purchases a warrant, and resides on the land should be required to be a British subject any more than a man who takes up an ordinary homestead. It will he a great mistake if the clause is left in its present shape. You will prevent a great many men who might wish to become purchasers from obtaining this land.
Say ' or makes tbe declaration to become a British subject.'
That would be better.

The law which applies to the ordinary homesteader would cover this case; he cannot get his patent unless he takes out his papers and becomes a British subject. I therefore move to strike out the words ' a British subject.'
Then a foreigner might come in and hold this land. Can a volunteer get his patent under this section without becoming a British subject?
Tbe same provision can be made as that which is contained in the Land Act.
He should be a British subject or be required to declare his intention of becoming one the same as a homesteader.
I do not think a homesteader has to make that declaration. I think it would be advisable to put in a provision that the patent should not issue to any one unless he is a British subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Turriff moves to strike out .the words ' a British subject.'
Some bon. MEMBERS. No, no.
I understand he has to be a British subject before be gets his patent.
No, it is tbe other way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to have the amendment explained.

I think there is a genera] misapprehension as to what I mean. I * propose to strike out the words that he must be a British subject in order to become a substitute for the original grantee, but I do not propose that he shall be allowed to receive the patent for the land until he becomes a British subject. Take the settler coming in from the United States ; he can take up a homestead but he does not become a British subject until he has lived three years in the country.
Has he not to declare ?
Let him make his declaration, and provide that before he gets the patent he must become a British subject.
Where we grant lauds to men because they went to fight for the British Crown no one should be allowed to speculate in these lands unless he is a British subject. The Bill is all right as it is.	,
ts McCarthy. Under the Lands Act we permit a man to make a homestead entry who has declared his intention, and why should there be any distinction made in this case?

I will ask that my amendment should read this way :
No person shall be accepted as a substitute unless he is a British subject or has declared his intention of becoming a British subject.
The whole idea of allowing a substitute in such a case as this is absurd. But if it be allowed it should be confined to a man who is already a British subject.
It should be provided that before receiving the patent he should become a British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no provision in
the section as it stands for a substitute becoming a British subject before getting his patent, and while I have no objection to the amendment as proposed, it should be followed by a provision that the substitute should be a British subject before he gets the patent.
Where is the necessity for this? Are there not sufficient British subjects to purchase these rights. It is ridiculous to extend this privilege to foreigners.

These scrips will undoubtedly be speculated in, and that being so, it is desirable to make them as valuable as possible. If we refuse to give the privilege to those who have not. yet taken out their naturalization papers we limit to that extent the market value of the scrip.

If I felt that these scrips were to be speculated in I would Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
vote against the whole Bill. We should approach this with the idea that British subjects should settle on these lands as far as possible. It is not like a foreigner coming in and taking up a homestead entry in the ordinary way. This is a special grant to certain brave and loyal British subjects whom we desire to honour and we should restrict it to British subjects.
We encourage foreigners to come here and declare their intention to become British subjects, and when they do so in good faith we ought not to restrict them in their privileges of citizenship.
I am quite content that such a one should have all the ordinary privileges of citizenship, but this is a special case altogether.

I would add to my
amendment the words :
And no patent shall issue for any lands under this Act until the holder has become a British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The difficulty could be met by adding to section 2 of the Bill the words:
The patent shall not issue until he has become a British subject.

Suppose John Smith
fought in South Africa and he sells his rights to Thomas Brown, who becomes his substitute ; could Thomas Brown sell his rights to another person?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. The Bill expressly says that the volunteers may sell to a substitute and the substitute must earn the patent.
No, it does not say that.

Every restriction we put on these grants is just lessening the value of the man who gets it. Our experience fi'om 1871 to 1875, when there was plenty of scrip in the market-and at that time anybody could buy it and there was no requirement that he should be a British subject-was that better prices were got than if there had been no restriction. Any restriction Is bound to lower the price to the man who holds the property.

This violates a very Important principle that we should not lose sight of, and that is the principle of settling these lands with people who are going to farm them. It is better to have four farmers farming 160 acres each than to have one farmer owning a farm of 640 acres. You are increasing the holdings to these settlers and in that way are keeping out settlement. I do not think the minister has looked Into this thing as he should. What we want to do is establish a population out there and not a few big land holders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not a peasant population.

I do not quite understand what the hon. gentleman means by ' a peasant population.' Do I understand the minister to say that a man with 160 acres is a peasant farmer? Does he want to establish a system of landlordism in that country? No man can possibly work 160 acres by himself. What the minister wants is to establish an aristocratic class who will have servants at their command. He desires to put the lauds of this country into the hands of a favoured few. What is the secret of the success of the French nation? It is the fact that the lands of France are divided up amongst small holders-a peasant class, if you will, but the bone and sinew of the French nation.	And if you call that a
peasant class, I would that we had in Canada a peasant class, for that is the class which is the salvation of France where the land is held by the men who work it and not by the employers of labour. I think a *very great mistake is being made when we allow any substitution and do not compel these men, who have, by their sacrifices in the past, earned their right to this land, to go out themselves and settle on it. For my part I protest against this policy in the interests of the people of the west as well as of the whole of Canada.
Do I understand the bon. geiitleman to protest against this land being given to the volunteers of South Africa?

If I have not made myself clear to the bright intellect of the hon. gentleman, it will be impossible, with the slight command I have of the English language, for me to use words which would convey my meaning to his intelligence. I am not opposing the grant to the South African veterans, but I am opposing the right of substitution which is attached to the grant and which is not in the interests of this country, because it will enable some of these men to sell for a song to the scrip shark, who has been the curse of the west and who has already his eyes fixed upon this Bill. There can be no doubt about that. The speculator who deals iu scrip is already looking to this Bill. He has not gorged himself quite full enough with the scrip of the halfbreed and is now after the scrip of the veteran. I say it is not in the interests of the west that large tracts of land should be held by individuals, but rather that smaller holdings should be the rule, and that there should be what my hon. friend the minister terms ' a peasant population ' rather than a population of rich landlords with servants and serfs at their command.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is under a misapprehension as to the purpose of this Bill. This Bill is not for the purpose of benefiting the west, and none know that better than the people who represent the west. It is supposed to be a discharge of the duty of the whole Dominion to those who went to
South Africa to serve the empire. This is a sacrifice on the part of the west and is recognized as such, but the west is prepared to do its part in recognizing the service of these men. It is useless to speak of this as though it were a benefit to the west. It is a case in which .the west is carrying the burden of the whole Dominion in making some recognition of the services of these men.

If that be true, better strike the Bill off the record altogether; and if it be necessary to provide some recognition for these veterans, we should do it by means of a money grant. This is only another illustration of the mistake we are committing in keeping the control of these lands in the federal government and not giving them to the provinces. What right have we to impose a sacrifice on the west? What right have we to do an act of injustice towards the west if, as the minister says, this is an act of injustice to that portion of our country. Let us from the Dominion treasury give these men proper remuneration for what they have done and not give an opportunity to the speculators to make a lot of money out of this grant, whereas our veterans will only get a very small portion of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not want to accept the suggestion, and have it put on record in ' Hansard,' that this is an injustice to the west.
That is what you said.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said it was a burden.
A burden is an injustice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily. It is a burden the people are quite prepared to bear. I want my hon. friend to understand that the honourable part which the west took in South Africa was a burden but not an injustice. It was a burden which the west bore proudly; and when we are doing what we can to recognize the services of these men in South Africa, we are acquitting a debt of honour and the west is proud to bear its share of that burden.
How many scrip can the speculator buy?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The speculator can buy as many scrip as he has money to pay for, but his scrip will only be of use to him if he can fulfil the duties and obligations required to earn the patent.

That means he will get a few more substitutes just as he had to produce the half-breed, and he did not always produce the half-breed he was supposed to produce. The minister says this is a burden on the west. In what respect? Is it because these lands are being granted ? Then why should the west bear the burden? Why should not the whole of Canada bear

it? If you make a money grant out of the Dominion treasury, the whole of Canada will bear the burden and not the west alone.
Mr, OLIVER. Precisely.
Why do you want to be unfair to the west? Is the west crying out for an opportunity to bear the burden? I have not heard the cry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The west is perhaps more willing to bear the burden than other parts of the country are willing to share it.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been no suggestion from any part of the country in the line my hon. friend suggested, that there should be a payment out of the treasury. It was a question of Northwest lands or nothing.

It is not necessarily a question of Northwest lands or nothing. There is no reason why some minister should not have brought down a Bill providing that a money grant should be given to the South African veterans.

According to the wording of this section, there might be more than one substitute, and the question is, which one would require to be a British subject. The first Substitute might dispose of his interest and go to the United States or anywhere else, and the last one who took tlie land would be the poor, downtrodden British subject who would have to fulfil the settlement duties. As the Bill stands, there can lie one or any number of substitutes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not wish to set up my knowledge of the law against that of the hon. gentleman ; but it is as plain as the English language can make it, that there is provision for an assignment to one substitute.

That does not limit it to one substitute. I do not think any lawyer will deny that the provision for a substitute must be taken as meaning any number of substitutes. If the section said 'one substitute,' that might limit it, but as it is it means his substitute for the time being. To my mind the section is all right unamended.

It seems to me that it would be a mistake to curtail the number of persons to whom those lands could be assigned ; because the man in the east cannot go and cultivate them, and any curtailment you put upon his right to dispose of them makes them of that much less value to him and therefore only weakens the object of them. I would allow as many substitutes as are allowed in the case of any commercial commodity. If this is not allowed, it would be better, as the hon. member for Kings and Albert suggests, that you should give these men a money grant. But I have not heard any such proposition before. Ever since I have been here, in every Mr. FOWLER.
session, the proposition has been to make grants of land to these South African veterans, and the powers that be have decided to give them lands. If you couple with the grant the condition that the grantee must go and settle on the land it will be absolutely useless to one-half or three-fourths of the men who went to South Africa.

I move that the. words ' twenty-one ' be struck out of the second line and the word ' eighteen ' be substituted therefor.
Amendment of Mr. Jackson agreed to.
On section 6-scrip may be granted instead of land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I desire to move that in the last line the word 1 nine ' be struck out and the word ' ten ' be substituted therefor.
If this Bill does not make it clear whether the substitute or the grantee has the right to assign, ought it not to be made clear ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to the question of an assignment by one substitute to another. I can only say that, so fa.r as I can read English, this provides for an assignment from the volunteers to a substitute, and the substitute must perform the duties. If the English language does not mean what it says, then an amendment would be necessary ; but that is the intent of the Act.

I quite agree with the hon. minister that if the English language is as he understands it and as I understand it, then an amendment is not necessary : but there are a number of lawyers in the House who claim that the language means what it does not appear to mean, [DOT] and I would, like to hear from them.

I moved that the following be inserted as section 6a :
Any person entitled to a grant of jand under the foregoing provisions may in lieu thereof if he so chooses, receive a free grant of one quarter-section without residence duties or homestead regulations, provided that he notifies the Minister of the Interior of his choice before December 31, 1910.
The object I have in view in moving this amendment is this. Certain men may prefer to take ICO acres of land and get a patent for the same without residing on the land. A great many men in the west who will be entitled to lands under this Act are in mercantile business, in stores, or in various occupations in town. Many more are ranchers or are engaged in some other occupation which they followed before the war broke out. Many of them would think it a great favour to be allowed to select a quarter-section of land and obtain the patent without further conditions. I would not suggest this as taking away from the rights of 1 those who choose the 320 acres but merely.

to provide for the man who wishes to take 160 acres without condition.
Amendment (Mr. Herron) negatived.

In reference to the provision that any transaction occurring before the issue of the scrip would be void,
is the minister prepared immediately to issue this scrip, or will that only come into effect after a certain date?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Bill will be in effect as soon as it is assented to.
When can application for warrants be made to the Minister of Militia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As soon as the Bill is
assented to.
When can the speculator begin to get in his work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not until the certificate has been issued to the volunteer.
The scrip must be issued on the application of the volunteer, not of the substitute?
Has the minister made an estimate of the number who will be likely to accept grants?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The number who would be entitled according to the present drafting of section 2 would be a little over 7,000, but if all the suggestions that have been made are followed the number will be very largely increased. I would be glad to have any further suggestions in regard to the provisions of section 2 before the committee rises. I would like to have the views of the committee with regard to the different classes of people who should be provided for. If we make the provisions of section 2 so wide and so general as to cover all the cases that have been suggested to the House, we are liable to have our Act subjected to abuses in administration that will probably defeat the object aimed at. If we made the Bill fairly restrictive, or did not widen it so much that it would be difficult to operate, the understanding being that special cases might be dealt with in a special Act, I think that would be a safer plan in the public interest than to undertake to cover all cases by a general provision.
Progress reported.

House in committee on Bill (No. 146) respecting proprietary medicines.-Mr. Tern-pieman.
On section 2-definitions.
Hon. WM, TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Inland Revenue). There is a custom in the trade that medicines are manufactured under contract for the proprietor. To meet that, I move to add the following as subsection (d ) :
WThere the manufacturer of a proprietary or patent medicine is not the proprietor

thereof, the proprietor who procures the same to be manufactured shall be deemed to be the manufacturer within the meaning of this Act.

Has the minister any further views with regard to the use of that word 'internal.' It was contended before the committee that it meant only what was introduced by the mouth, that anything taken through the nose, or a hypodermic injection of cocaine through the skin, might not come under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not know that the doctors would agree upon what ' internal ' means. I was surprised to be told that an injection by the nose was not considered an internal remedy. This Bill proposes to deal only with medicines taken internally.
On section 7-prohibited medicines.
I would like to ask the minister if he proposes to introduce a section which will make provision for the sale of such stock as druggists may have on hand at the time of the passing of this Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a point I gave some consideration to and, in discussing the matter with others, it was thought that under clause 17, where power is given to the Governor in Council to ' make such regulations for giving effect to any of the provisions of this Act and declaring the true intent thereof, in any case of doubt, as to him seems meet,' we may make regulations governing the sale of those medicines that may be in stock at the time this Act comes into force which would not be labelled in accordance with the Act. It is not at all probable that this Act will be brought into force before the first of the year, which will give dealers six months to prepare their labels in conformity with the Act and to dispose of their present stock. We do not contemplate to cause the trade any trouble in changing from the old to the new system. That point can be guarded against by regulation.

The minister has perhaps not thought of the fact that in a a great many cases druggists do not know the contents of their patent medicines, and it will be impossible to get rid of their stock at the expiration of the time mentioned by him. I think there should be some special provision to allow them to dispose of all the patent medicines that are on their hands at the time the Act is put into force. They might be compelled1 to put a date upon the bottle to show that it was manufactured before the Act passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: A special label ?

Yes, a special label. It would be impossible to put labels on the stock that they have in their drug stores to Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
indicate what the actual contents of the bottles are, because druggists would not know' what these were themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am of opinion that I have authority to require them to put a special label on the quantity that may be in stock at the present time, or to label it as nearly as possible in conformity with this Act.

If you could compel them to put some special label on to show that the stock was manufactured before the Act came into force it would save them from losing their stock. We would not wish to do any injury to those who have laid in a large stock. Frequently druggists buy a large stock of a particular kind of patent medicine which is used in their neighbourhood. They get a discount if they take a large amount, and if some provision were not made such as I suggest an injury might be done to local druggists throughout the country.

Many drug stores have these patent medicines on their shelves for probably two or three years. Giving them until next January would afford them no opportunity w'liatever to dispose of their stock. I think it is a question that should be carefully guarded. It is absolutely necessary that a restriction should be imposed which would prevent them from selling year after year or from buying more stock and selling it under the pretence that it w'as the stock which they originally had on hand. A great injustice might be done to the druggists who have a stock of patent medicines on hand unless provision is made which wall enable them to dispose of it.
On section 9-distribution from door to door.

I W'ould like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that in schedule (a) there are three or perhaps more coal tar products mentioned, but there are several others that might as well be included.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The schedule was prepared by the chemist of the department but it may not be complete. Under clause 17 it w'ill be seen that we can add to or remove from schedule 1A ' any poisonous or patent drugs as from time to time may be deemed expedient. One of the first things that would be done after this became law would be to complete that schedule and issue a circular.
Mi-. DANIEL. I think this schedule would be more satisfactory if instead of mentioning a few of these coal tar products it should include all coal tar products. Why should a acetanilide be included in the schedule and antipyrine left out. If you are going to include any of these coal tar products you should include them ail.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Are all coal tar products poisonous ?

One is perhaps not so bad as another but they are all of the same character and liave the same effect. The Bill at present really puts a ban on these mentioned and gives an advertisement to those that are not mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: What are they ?

As it happens those that are not mentioned are largely proprietary. For instance, antikamnia which is said to be an extract of acetanilide and bicarbonate of soda but the basis of it is aeetana-lide. It is sold under the trade name of antikamnia and would not come under this Bill. It is the same with antipyrine which I believe is made in Germany and which is also proprietary. It is a coal tar product just the same as acetanalide and phenace-tine. Those that are not mentioned by name in the Blli are in the same category as those which are, and they should only be taken under advice.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Would you suggest that the Bill should say : Acetanalide and other coal tar products ?
I would put It In that way.
These coal tar products all affect the heart and are exceedingly dangerous medicine.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Before putting the Bill in force I presume this matter would be submitted to the proper authorities. It is my intention that it should be submitted to some eminent medical man so that we might get a complete list, and in the meantime we can insert the words : ' and other coal tar products.'

The trouble about inserting a complete list in a statute is that they are constantly getting out new coal tar products and describing them by some trade name. The minister in the schedule puts a ban on certain preparations and at the same time gives an immense advertisement to other preparations which are largely proprietary, such as antipyrine and antikamnia, to which exactly the same objections apply. I think it would be only fair and right, both to the public and to the people dealing in these things, that the general term should be used instead of these individual terms, unless you see the individual names of all the preparations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are there not coal tar products which are not of a medicinal character? If so, would it not be wise to say ' and all other coal tar products used for medicinal purposes ' ? Otherwise you would make it too comprehensive.
That would not be necessary as the Bill applies only to preparations used as medicines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I move that the words ' and other coal tar products ' be added to the schedule.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I would like to ask the minister if he has been able to devise any plan for putting a limit to certain advertisements of medicines or remedies that are not at all reputable? I think I need not enter more particularly into a description of them ; they will suggest themselves. These advertisements have appeared from time to time in some newspapers which are not over particular, and it would be well, if possible, to put some limit upon them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a point which has been considered. The practice of publishing advertisements of patent medicines that are not of a creditable character has been, I was going to say, universal ; but in recent years, I am bound to say, there has been a great improvement in that regard. Public opinion has put a ban on that class of advertising, and it is not nearly so commonly in vogue now as it was formerly. I had an amendment drafted prohibiting obscene advertising, but I recognized the difficulty and also the danger of trying to exercise a censorship over advertising of any kind. I did ask the Department of Justice some days ago how far we could go in prohibiting obscene or objectionable advertising of patent medicines, but the Department of Justice, up to the present time, has not helped me out. So I thought it better to let this Bill become law without referring to advertising at all. As I have said, the evil is not nearly so great as it used to be. The press of Canada has refused to carry in its columns advertising of that character, and I do not know that it would be wise to attempt to legislate on the subject in this Bill. I am afraid that we might have some difficulty in enforcing such legislation, and I am not prepared to draw the line between what should and what should not be published. I think that this measure, which is not very drastic, is along the right lines, and after we give it a fair trial for a year or two, we can perhaps devise a clause to regulate such advertising.
The minister has in the schedule a basis for regulating all such matters. By enlarging the schedule he can overcome to a great extent the evil complained of.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I observe that the minister, in section 14, subsection 2, appears to contemplate some kind of third party procedure. I am not quite sure that will work



1262S
out satisfactorily. What is contemplated exactly by subsection 2 of section 14 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In the Bill as first printed we had incorporated a warranty clause, requiring the giving of a warranty by the manufacturer to the vendor. We thought it would be very cumbersome to have that warranty accompanying every sale of goods, and we substituted clause 14, which is an entirely new clause, approved of by the special committee. If my hon. friend will look at the latter part of section 14 he will see that the manufacturer's name and number must be given on the label and that is sufficient identification of the manufacturer for the purposes of the section, and he can be brought in as the defendant in a prosecution. The action will then be brought against the manufacturer and the court will find, if the offence be proved, against the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There may be some provision in the Summary Conviction Act which provides that the defendant can obtain a summons to bring a third person before the court, but unless there is, this subsection could not be worked out. Can the minister tell me if there is any such provision ? The subsection reads :
2. If the person who gives notice of such defence, or the prosecutor, obtains a summons to bring such third party before the court, the court shall at the same time hear all the parties and decide upon the entire merits of the case, not only as regards the person originally accused hut also as regards the third party so brought before the court.

I do not think there is any such provision in the sense the hon. gentleman refers to. There Js in civil proceedings. What I should judge this to mean is that the defendant, in order to exonerate himself, must institute a new proceeding against the third party, which would really be a separate prosecution. If he wants to clear himself, he [DOT] should lay information against the party responsible and prove his charge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In some provinces there is a provision for bringing in a third party in civil cases, in others there is not, and this applies to the whole of Canada. Even If this were intended to apply to civil proceedings alone, I do not think it would work out very satisfactorily. But in a criminal proceeding, I do not see how you could work it out at all. There will be two different prosecutions, and the bald statement that ' the court shall at the same time hear all the parties and decide upon the entire merits of the case,' would be a little too general to enable the provisions of this section to be worked out at all. Is it contemplated, for example, that the magistrate would give the one judgment in the two cases and that this section will be sufficient Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
for that to he done ? I would hardly think so
There is another way in which it could be done. The proceedings could be amended by making the manufacturer a defendant along *with the other party. It is, of course open to some objection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We have not the time to work it out and it is not of sufficient importance to insist upon. No doubt the Bill will have to be amended.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved second reading of Bill (No. 202) to authorize the construction of a branch line of the Prince Edward Island Railway from Harmony, on the Souris branch, to Elmira. He said : This is for the purpose of taking authority, if the government so desire, to build a line, a little over thirteen miles long, from Harmony, on the Souris branch, to Elmira. It will serve a very important country, where there are several sections thickly settled which are without railway communication. The road will cost probably in the vicinity of $400,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Might I ask whether or not there were some other proposed branches which seem to have been agitated for in Prince Edward Island for a number of years? When I visited the island three or four years ago, I heard of several of these branches which seemed to 'be on much the same basis as regards their claims on the exchequer. Why has this particular branch been selected and the others put to one side ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: The government is of the opinion that this is all we can undertake this year. Some branch had to be selected, and I suppose the same question would be asked of any branch. Two branches were asked for in this vicinity. The Prince Edward Island legislature passed a resolution in which they named several branches and this was one.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: In whose county is it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: It does not say in my brief which county it is in,_ The resolution passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island referred to many branch lines.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Has the minister that' resolution with him ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: He will find it includes many lines in addition to the little bit of a paltry spur line he proposes.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I wish to again refer to the whole question of branch lines in connection with the government system of railways in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Would that not be an irrelevant matter?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I think it is germane to this Bill. It is a branch line being constructed by the government, the others are branch lines connected with the government system and the one question is involved in the other. It seems to me that the government, before constructing new branch lines in Prince Edward Island or any other province should consider and deal with the branch lines already in existence connecting with the government system. The Dominion has expended in connection with the several branch lines throughout the provinces traversed by the Intercolonial Railway nearly $7,000,000. The provinces have contributed to the same end about $5,000,000. The branch lines thus added by this parliament are all designed for one purpose, evidently we must assume that they are for the purpose of promoting the interests of the several communities traversed by them.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I do not like to raise a point of order, but I am forced to. I do not see the bearing of branch lines in other provinces on the Bill under discussion.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I submit I am in order ; I am arguing that before such a Bill is proceeded with the government should deal with the question of branch lines already constructed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I am rather inclined to think that a general discussion of branch lines in other provinces is hardly relative to a motion for the second reading of a particular Bill which deals with a particular branch line in one province. Beyond that the hon. member will see he is reviving a discussion which has already taken place in this House in this session at his own instance on the same question.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Of course I submit with all deference to the ruling of the Chair.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I think a discussion as to whether or not this branch line should be constructed is germane, but not a discussion of other branch lines in other provinces.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
I do not propose to deal with other branch lines in other provinces, but I do propose to show reasons why the government should not deal with this particular branch line at this stage. Parliament, before committing itself to an expenditure of $400,000 or $500,000, should inquire into the question of whether the expenditure already made in the past in 401*
connection with branch lines has been effectually made and has been made to accomplish the object which parliament evidently had in view, that is the benefit of the communities traversed by other branch lines.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: The hon. member has paid no attention to your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I think thus far the hon. member is paying attention to the ruling.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: They are only building this on paper for election purposes.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
I am dealing with this on principle. There is no narrow pent-up Utica of partisanship that will confine my views at this time. When this Bill has passed both Houses and has received the assent of His Excellency the responsibility will be on the government, but at present it is on parliament. The question is : Should parliament authorize the government of Canada to construct even a small branch line like this of only thirteen miles until parliament has dealt with the wider and greater question with respect to branch lines already in existence?
I have no particular objection to this branch line. Jly hon. friend the Minister of Railways has referred to the fact that the legislature of Prince Edward Island has passed a resolution, unanimously I assume, in favour of the construction of this particular line, and other lines, and that resolution no doubt called upon this parliament to authorize the construction of this particular branch line as well as others mentioned in that resolution. In considering that request, it seems to me to be the bounden duty of parliament to inquire whether this authority should be given until this parliament has dealt with the branch lines already existing in a way that would make them fulfil the respective missions which it was expected they would fulfil when parliament authorized their construction. The same question would arise if we were asked to subsidize an additional branch line in connection with the government system of railways on the main line of the Intercolonial Railway. This, I understand, to be an extension of the government system, and you cannot separate it. Because it happens to be in the province of Prince Edward Island is no reason why it should be separated from the whole system of the government railways of the Dominion. Should that be extended, should there be a draft made upon the revenues of Canada to create additional lines to the system until that system is placed in a position whereby it would fulfil the aspirations and hopes of the people when that system was constructed? I submit I am in order. I bow to your ruling, but I do not think I am departing from your ruling. I .submit that the Minister of Railways, who cf course spoke for the government with respect to their policy in that regard, should give some idea as re-

gards the course to be pursued iu connection with branch lines already existing before asking us to deal with the proposition involved in the Bill now before the House. I hope I have made myself clear, and I hope the Minister of Railways will see the point of the objection I take to the Bill at this moment.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
I think that is a very lame excuse, it is the lamest excuse I ever heard this minister make. These are hardly branch lines, they are only spurs. Mr. EMMERSON

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.

Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) a few years ago when he was in Prince Edward Island w'ith the tariff commission. speechtext:
This bears on the question that the minister took
