maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Allusion can be made to it but it is not the question before the chair.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: There is the agreement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: The question before the chair lias reference to the construction of the Elmira branch.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I hope I am in order. The minister says they do not want to proceed with the New London branch because there is a disagreement about routes. Here is the agreement that they entered into, signed by representatives of the different sections, and it shows that there was a perfect unanimity. I believe that we are going to have an exhibition of the same character as that which we had previous to the election of 1904. We are now in the last session of parliament, I presume, and the Bill is introduced to construct a few miles of railway in Kings county for the benefit of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes). I believe it is only on paper.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Your belief is very active.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
Yes, very active. In 1904 they pursued a different course. They began surveys all over the province. They began to survey this very railway and the minister says there is a disagreement about the New London branch. If there is a disagreement about the route, of the New London branch there is also a disagreement about this one. I know something of the history of these railways and there was a pretty free fight with regard to the proposed route of the Elmira branch. Here is a statement about the surveys we had in 1904-in 1904 and it is 1908. four years ago. I made the statement in the early part of the session that the hon. member for Kings had said that unless this branch was built within a year he would resign his seat. He contradicted me, he said the statement was not true. I believe he said two years in place of one. But, four years have gone and it is safe enough to come in with a Bill now at the end of a term of parliament and say that they are going to proceed with that. line. This is a different procedure from that of 1904. Here is a return which I asked for and which will be given an idea to the House of how they spend money in order to carry elections and for the people of Prince Edward Island. There is the survey of this Elmira branch costing $1,500 ; there is the survey of the New London branch, costing $1,500 ; there is the survey of the main line to the west shore near O'Leary costing $1,500. That is the way
the money goes. What do they give to the people of Prince Edward Island for all this expenditure ? The minister says that they cannot proceed with the New London branch. I wanted to quote the agreement that was entered into but the chairman ruled me out of order. I bow to the decision of the chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman was going into details about the New London branch.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
If this Bill on paper is going to help the return of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) I do not think I should oppose it, but I must say it comes far short of what Prince Edward Island requires. The Minister of Railways laid great emphasis on a petition from the legislature of Prince Edward Island, and that legislature is of the same political stripe as the Minister of Railways, and if he had so much confidence in that petition as he pretends to have. I rather think he would carry out the prayer of the whole petition and not simply a small part of it. The Conservative government, in 1896, prepared a comprehensive Bill which would satisfy the province' of Prince .Edward Island in regard to branch railways. In consideration of the fact that the original railway on Prince Edward Island was paid for by the province the Conservative government decided in 1896 that 106 miles of branch railways should be built; and, mind you, they came to that conclusion when the revenue of Canada was only $40,000,000, while now the expenditure is $126,000,000. Why, this Liberal government spent as much money on the few miles of railway they have built in Prince Edward Island as would have equipped the whole province with every mile of railway the people want if the money were wisely expended. The Conservative government, in 1896, knew that the people of Prince Edward Island were coming to the government year after year for a branch railway, and they asked the people to state exactly what the province required, and the people of Prince Edward Island came to an understanding as to what was required, and the government embodied it in a resolution submitted to this parliament. The resolution moved by Mr. Haggart in 1896 was as follows :
Mr. Haggart moved that the House resolve itself into com m 1 It ee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to build and operate as part of the Prince Edward Island Railway the following lines of railway, that is to say:
(a)	From Southport to Murray harbour south with cross line connecting with the Prince Edward Island Railway between New Perth and Cardigan stations touching at or near Montague bridge.

That is the only line this government has undertaken, and it is not completed yet.
(b)	From Souris or Harmony station to Elmira.
(c)	From a point beween Loyalty junction and York station to Cove head, and thence to Oyster bed bridge.
That is one of the finest sections of country in the province, and the railway would reach the best fishing grounds and would afford the very best feeder for the main line. The branch this government did build is making money, and in consequence of it the deficit on the Prince Edward Island Railway is decreasing year by year. If you extend it to Rustico and New London, as the Conservative party proposed to do in 1S9G, I believe that in a few years the deficit on the Prince Edward Island Railway would be entirely wiped out.
*(d) From Emerald junction to Stanley bridge touching at or near Clifton.
(e)	From Summerside to Richmond bay.
(f)	From some point at or near O'Leary's station to some point ion the western coast between Brae and Cape Wolfe.
(g)	From Wiltshire to Victoria.
All those branches would only amount to about 106 miles, and it was estimated at the time that their cost would be $1,088,000.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: That is on paper.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Your Bill is on paper too and you may be on paper yourself pretty soon. Now, these 106 miles could be built for something over $1,000,000, and yet this government built about 60 miles which cost them nearly $2,00,000.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: 1. HUGHES. That is simply incorrect.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.

speechtext:
That was a comprehensive Bill which would have settled the whole trouble in Prince Edward Island. As I said before, a huge mistake was made for the province when the original cost of the railway was charged in its debt account with Canada. The Conservative party said that in consideration of that large sum of money, three and one-quarter millions, being charged against the province, the best way to expend it would be to give the province railway accommodation, and if the Conservative party had been returned to carry out that policy, I believe that all these branches would have been built to-day at no greater expense than the few lines that have been completed.
Mr. MARTIN (Queens, P.li I )

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Some time ago I put some questions on the Order Paper with reference to the New London branch of this railway, and they were answered by the Minister of Railways. In the year 1904 a survey was made of the New London branch and the lion. Finance Minister, when acting as Minister of Railways, promised to do everything in his power to build that branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: No. My hon. friend is not serious when he talks of the Minister of Finance promising to build railways.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I will just read a copy of a return dated 1904, and I think the Finance Minister will change his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: No, I did not promise anything.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
I believe the present government will promise anything, especially when an election is coming on. Here is a letter dated Moncton, N.B., the 1st of August, 1904, and signed by D. Pot-tinger, an officer of the government, with reference to the New London branch, the Elmira branch and the O'Leary branch. This letter states that $1,500 would be the cost of a survey of each of these branches, and at the end it reads as follows :
All these amounts will have to he expended before the 30th June next, so it is important that the works should be got ready for tendering as soon as possible.
Why did they want these works to be tendered for before the 30th of June, 1904? Because they intended to issue the writs for an election, and wanted these tenders to be out to deceive the people. They did not intend to go on with any of these works, and they do not intend to-day to have any contract for the Elmira branch any more than they did for these three branch lines. This letter goes on to say :
If you require any more people to attend to this, please let me know, and I will ask Air. Schreiber to give me the names of some that he says he has on his lists here.
He wanted some men to go out and tell tlie people that the government were going to build these branches, but there were never any contracts issued for that purpose. In March, 1908, I asked the Alinister of Railways this question :
1. Did the government receive petitions from inhabitants of Clifton, Stanley and Hope River, Prince Edward Island, praying for extension of railway from the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway to Stanley Bridge or vicinity, and for the placing of a sum sufficient for the purpose in this year's estimates ?
The answer was :	' Yes.' He received
those petitions, and lie received petitions also in 1904, and the Alinister of Finance

said iu 1900 that he would appoint a competent engineer, an independent man, to go and make a survey of these branch lines, but no survey has been made up to the present day. The next question was:
Is it the intention of the government to grant the prayer of the petitions?
The answer was : ' The government has not so decided.' The third question I asked was :
Is it the intention of the government to make surveys this year with. a view to extend the railway system along the north shore of Prince Edward Island?
The answer was : ' No decision has been reached.' Although the Minister of Railways gave this answer in March last, I presume that he has not considered the matter even up to the present time. I would ask him now if he has reached a decision with reference to the construction of a railway on the north shore of Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: My hon. friend has named several railways. What railway does he now refer to?

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: The New London branch.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Will the minister say that work has been done yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was asking me if it had been considered. I was replying to his question.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
The question is this:
Is it the intention of the government to make surveys this year with a view to extend the railway system along the north shore of Prince Edward Island?
Will the minister answrer that question now ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Yes. It is the intention of the government to comply with the request of my hon. friend and to meet his complaint that no independent survey has been made of what is known as the new London branch. Whether it will be built or not is a matter for future consideration, because I will not build any railway until I am satisfied that it is in the interest of the public and ought to be constructed.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: Then I will ask the minister if lie has read the report of tne engineers who made the survey of the New London branch line in 1901 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I have not.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
I do not think the minister takes very much interest in the construction of this railway. The railways which lie now contemplates building are simply political railways. I do not object to the building of a railway from the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway to Elmira. I think it is necessary in the interest of the people that that railway should be built, but I think there is a railway which should be built in preference to that, namely, the railway along the north shore of the island. The people there last year, as I have stated before in this House, ou account of the weather which existed in the province, were unable to ship any of their produce until after the winter season came, and as a result they were put to great inconvenience and loss. If there had been a railway on the north shore, they would have been able to sell their grain and other produce like other people in the province. You are building the Grand Trunk Pacific at a cost of $250,000,000, and you contemplate building the Georgian Bay canal at a cost of $90,000,000 and the Hudson Bay Railway at a cost of $90,000,000 or $100,000,000 where there is not one workman living, while in Prince Edward Island and in the settled portions of Nova Scotia there are people living who have been for a hundred years without any railways at all. Why does this state of affairs' exist ?
You go up here 150 miles north of the Ottawa, in some cases 200 miles, where there is not a man living, and you build a railway at the expense of the people where there will not be a white man living for the next ten or twenty years, and where no railway can get any traffic. Why do you build these lines? * That is the question asked by every man in Canada and the government cannot give any answer. These places will never be settled except in some spots where the lands are good, but where we have land settled, on which people have been living over a hundred years-places which are the most thickly settled portions of Canada to-day, with fifty-five people to the mile-you will not give us any railway. Our sons go out to the Northwest. Why? Because they have not got the railway communication they should have at home. But when they go out to the northwest, they settle near a railway, and they will be very apt to go near where there is a railway, because they . know the government are spending money for the few people living in the west in order that they may get their votes. At the next general elections however the government will be disappointed at the result of their policy, for our people are sufficiently intelligent and patriotic to know that their own homes should be provided with railway communication by the government and let those people who go out west take pot luck the same as those in the east have had to do up to the present. We are spending millions of dollars on Russians and Galicians

out in the Northwest and are leaving the Scotch and the Irish and the English to get along as best they can in the east without government assistance. Our people in the east have to haul their produce some twenty five or thirty miles to market, and in many sections in Prince Edward Island they have no markets in which to sell their produce at all which they can reach with any convenience. The policy of the government is unfair to the people of the east. The east is neglected in favour of the west. The west is getting it all. What has been the condition of affairs in this House during this session? Two-thirds of our time has been taken up with the affairs of the Northwest and of Ontario, and millions of dollars have been spent in the west compared with only thousands in the east. It is true that we have one hundred and seventy-eight items to-day in the estimates for Nova Scotia, but that does not amount to very much. That is only an election dodge. We have only a few items for Prince Edward Island, and the time will soon come when the First Minister will regret the stand he has taken with reference to the east. It is time for him to look to the east and leave the west alone. They have enough. Millions of dollars have been spent and mis-spent in the west, some of which should have gone to the east, and it is time the government realized that fact. It is time the government should take in the branch lines which the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) is interested in. I believe that probably we shall take in those branch lines, but we should build some railways for the people who have built up Canada. We should not concede everything that the people of the west ask for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I am much obliged to my hon. friend for the testimony he has given of what the government are doing in the west, and no doubt in the west he includes the middle country, the great province of Ontario. Altogether too much of our time is taken up in debating these matters from a sectional point of view. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that the maritime provinces are getting too much and their press circulates the story that this government is favouring the maritime provinces. The speech of the hon. gentleman is a good answer to that charge and no doubt will be made use of.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) The hon. members for Queens, P.E.I., appear very anxious to get the people of Prince Edward Island to think that the construction of the branch line from Harmony to Elmira will only be on paper and that the government is not sincere. Well, this government has shown its sincerity by its action in the building of railways in Prince Edward Island and other improvements in that province. The senior member from Queens County (Mr. Alex. Martin) condemned the government because it only built sixty miles Mr. A. A. McLEAN.
of railway in that province the last few years, but that is far more than the previous government did. The late government brought in a resolution on April 21, 1906, when parliament was about to expire by efflux of time on the 23rd of that month, to build seven or eight branches of railway on the island, and parliament had only two days in which to consider that and many other matters, and the subject was never mentioned again. But this government proceeds in another and different way. It brings in its Bills to build railways, passes them through the committee stage and makes them the law of the land, and puts the money in the estimates. That is what has been done in this case and in addition we have the word of the Minister of Railways that this branch will be proceeded with this summer.
Now let me say a word or two with regard to the senior member for Queens county, who seems to take special delight in overstating the cost of the Murray harbour branch. Why he does this, I cannot imagine except that he wishes to prejudice the construction of railways in our province in the minds of members from the other provinces. I can know of no other reason. He lias repeatedly made the statement this session, which is absolutely incorrect, that the Murray Harbour branch cost over $31,000 a mile or $2,000,000. When I denied that, he asked me if I could give him the figures, and I am now in a position to give them. The total cost of that branch line, including rolling stock, stations, sidings and everything else, was $1,255,495.59 or $23,782.83 per mile, which is about one-third less than the statement made by him. But that is about as near the facts as he generally gets.
My hon. friend the senior member for Queens (Mr. Martin) professes great anxiety for the extension of the Montague branch until it would connect with the Murray Harbour line. I have just to remind him that some two years ago, when I was pressing that matter on the attention of the government, he was the very man who came in with the interruption that I was asking for too much.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: You were going to Murray river at that time.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: I was stating that the connection should be made with the line to Murray Harbour.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: You said Murray river.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext: That statement is about as near the facts as nay hon. friend manages to get. That is all I have to say with regard to this matter. This project of an extension of the railway from Harmony to Elmira is bona fide. The line will be constructed. The present government and Minister of Railways are the men to do what they say, and my hon. friend can possess his soul in patience.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND RAILWAY-HARMONY TO ELMIRA BRANCH.
speechtext:
This is a death-bed repentance on the part of the government with regard to this branch line to Elmira. I do not think it will go down very much with the people, but he thinks he will get a few votes on the head of it.
The Murray Harbour Railway seems to be troubling him. I said it cost nearly $2,000,000 and he questioned that.

speechtext: In this Bill we change the salary and we insert a section for the purpose of preserving to the Auditor General the right of promotion which, under the existing law, belongs to him now, so that there may be no change in that respect. The Governor in Council makes the appointments, but promotions have always been within the authority of the Auditor General, and as it seems that under the new Civil Service Act there may be some doubt in that respect, we are making it clear.
Is that the right of promotion personally or the promotion of the clerks in his office ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The promotion of his clerks. The office of the Auditor General, being regarded as somewhat different from an ordinary departmental office, the practice in the past has been that he should be allowed to make promotions. It would come as my duty to report these promotions to council, but I have no voice in making them. We preserve that right to him because he is an officer of parliament and not an ordinary departmental officer. This is the law now and, as the civil service law might interfere with it, we preserve the right of promotion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Canada Shipping Act, chapiter 113, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, by repealing section 958 and substituting therefor-
958. The Governor in Council may from time to time,
(a) by order in council declare that the foregoing provisions of this part shall not, while such order in council is in force, apply, either throughout Canada or in any specified waiters of Canada, to the ships or vessels, or to any specified ascertained or ascertainable class or number of the ships or vessels of any foreign country in which British ships are admitted to the coasting trade of such country, and to carry goods or passengers from one port to another in such country; and
(b) revoke or vary such order in counoil.
2.	That the Act founded on this resolution shall not oonne into force until His Majesty's pleasure thereon has been signified by publication in the ' Canada Gazette.'-Mr. Fielding.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We will take the resolution now and the discussion can take place upon the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so. '
What is the explanation of this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of the BUI may be briefly stated. We have been granting coasting privileges to the ships of a number of foreign nations which in return have given us the privilege of coasting in their own land. There is nothing in this Bill about American vessels because the United States do not give us coasting privileges. However, in the case of Norway for instance, we have no coasting trade there and the privilege they give Is no advantage to us. Norway, on the other band, has been making much use of our coasting trade and the complaint is that our native vessels are placed at a disadvantage in that respect. An order in council some months ago provided that on the 1st of January next the privileges granted to these various countries, including Norway, should be cancelled and that thereafter their vessels should not be entitled to our coasting trade. We will probably all agree that is a desirable policy. But it has been represented to ns by the coal companies that this would be a hardship upon them. They say the Norwegians have been supplying vessels of a special class intended for the coal trade and that if we should suddenly determine that these vessels are to he shut out of the coasting trade it will not be possible for them in the short time allowed to find either Canadian vessels or British vessels to do the work. They also say they have a number of vessels which have been chartered for several years, and the cancellation of these charters would be a very serious loss to them. It has been suggested that we might meet their views by giving them the privilege of employing vessels of a certain class which do not come into competition with Canadian vessels. We have discovered that under the existing law, while we have the power to shut out foreign vessels altogether, we have not the power to say that a particular class of these vessels shall he admitted. What we propose by this legislation is to give the government the power not only to exclude them altogether, but to discriminate and to say th:it we may admit vessels of a certain class, these being the vessels which do not come into competition with Canadian vessels. We might allow them the coasting trade for a limited time until arrangements can he made to supply their places With British vessels. We could not even say un-

tier the present law that we would admit a vessel to the coasting trade of the Atlantic but not to the coasting trade qf the Pacific, or the great lakes, and so on. This legislation proposes that there should be elasticity to enable the government to meet the particular conditions as they arise. The general policy of the government is to exclude these vessels from the coasting trade, but under this amendment, which cannot take effect until authorized by the imperial authorities, we would have the power to make exceptions for a limited time if we so desire in such cases as I have mentioned.
Will the class of vessels be decided on by the tonnage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Either steam or sail?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no distinction in the law as respects steam or sail.
Under this the government would be able to allow Norwegian vessels of a certain tonnage to engage in the coasting trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And exclude these of a smaller tonnage.
I presume wo have no Canadian vessels to do the trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in the case of the larger vessels, certainly.
Is it a fact that these vessels are manned by Norwegians?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think so.
Is it a fact that year in and year out they do a Canadian coasting business ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, the coal trade is largely handled by them. In some cases they are of English build for Norwegian account, owned and manned by Norwegians and under the Norwegian flag ; sometimes they are owned by Englishmen but sail under the Norwegian flag and so are treated as foreigners.
Mr, STANFIELD. I notice in the newspapers that these foreign steamers are given a preference over Canadian ships in loading at the coal mines. Could not we protect those Canadian vessels in this legislation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a different question from the one dealt with by this Bill. The complaint there is that steamers are given preference over sailing ships and the steamers would be given preference whether they were British or Norwegians. I believe there was considerable trouble about that matter, but I am advised it is all adjusted now and that there is no complaint.

I have a long letter from a sea captain resident in Westmore-Mr. FIELDING.
land who sails a British vessel and his great complaint is that his vessel was discriminated against in favour of the Norwegian steamers. In that way, if this permission is given, there is some ground for the exception taken. I am not familiar with the circumstances myself, but it seemed to be a matter for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I submitted the complaint to that department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is not a question of discrimination between the Cana-liau vessel and the Norwegian vessel, but a question between the sailing vessel and the steamer. However, while there was some cause of complaint in the past, I understand that it has been largely, if not wholly, removed.

The Minister of Finance states that Norwegian vessels have been chartered for the coal trade for several years. I want to know whether that is the reason for the passing of this Act, because I think that these Norwegians should not control the shipping trade of the maritime provinces as they do to-day.
Nonsense.

I know that is correct. I do not care whether it is Sydney, or Inverness, or Pietou ; and I tell the Minister of Finance that he should not take the opinion of men who are interested in one particular locality. He knows that the men engaged in this business cannot get a cargo if a Norwegian vessel intervenes, whether it is half loaded or fully loaded.

I rise for the purpose of letting my hon. friend know that his information is entirely incorrect, for this reason, that having been in my county within the last two weeks and knowing that my hon. friend and some other gentlemen here had been complaining of the difficulty of schooners from Prince Edward Island and elsewhere getting coal expeditiously, the managers of both mining companies informed me that there had not been the slightest delay in the shipments of coal from any of the piers by any schooners that came there so far this summer. In fact, they were anxious to get the trade and to deal expeditiously with any schooners that came there. We have two large piers capable of supplying more coal per day than all the schooners of Prince Edward Island could possibly engage in carrying. If my hon. friend will give me a bona fide case of any schooner from Prince Edward Island which has been delayed with a shipment of coal in my county, I will undertake to see that there is a remedy.
I can assure him that all the complaints in ^hat regard, so far as Pietou is concerned, are entirely incorrect. There was some difficulty in regard to shipments from the

Inverness Coal Company, and an agitation was worked up on that account; but any complaints with regard to the shipment of coal from the Dominion Coal Company, or from the county of Pietou, are not well founded.
